tier_reason: The paper was peer-reviewed (IEEE TIFS 2025), but its reference-Falcon baseline figures (5,948.1 sign/s, 27,933.0 verify/s) were copied from falcon-sign.info (i5-8259U, compiler flags not given) rather than re-run. The GPU-vs-single-core-CPU gains are 70.65x/369.13x, over 50x with the baseline flags unstated, so the implausible-ratio rule caps the tier at C. No code is linked from the paper.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Falcon on RTX 4090: 420.25 kops/s signing (Table II: 420,250.10 ops/s) and 10,311.04 kops/s verification. The '42.02 kops/s' in the ePrint web abstract is a typo; the PDF abstract and Table II both say 420.25. Against the reference Falcon figures from falcon-sign.info (i5-8259U) the gain is 70.65x signing / 369.13x verification (the paper's '70.65x to 369.13x', Sec. IV-E). The abstract's 58.05x/73.14x is actually against the fastest CPU implementation (Nguyen et al., Apple M1), as Sec. IV-E and the conclusion show. GOLF is also 7.17x/3.79x over the fastest prior GPU work (Lee et al., on an A100, so different hardware) and 2.69x/1.53x on the same A100.
corrections.baseline: Falcon reference implementation throughput as published on falcon-sign.info (Intel Core i5-8259U @ 2.3 GHz, TurboBoost off), cited as Fouque et al. (Ref) in Table II and not re-run by the authors; also prior CPU/GPU Falcon papers
corrections.hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24 GB) with an AMD Ryzen 7 5700G host; also tested on an NVIDIA A100. The reference baseline numbers come from the Falcon website on an Intel Core i5-8259U (the paper's text also says i5-8279U).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: NVCC, CUDA 12.1, -rdc=true -arch sm_89 -maxrregcount=127 (GPU side); the reference baseline's compiler and flags are not stated (numbers copied from falcon-sign.info)
corrections.workload: Batch Falcon signature generation and verification throughput (ops/s) on an RTX 4090 (and an A100), compared with the Falcon reference implementation's published single-machine CPU throughput and with prior CPU/GPU Falcon implementations (Table II)
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed as IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security vol. 20, pp. 9441-9453 (2025), doi:10.1109/TIFS.2025.3599681; the ePrint copy is labelled Preprint. The reference baseline was copied from the Falcon website (different CPU, flags unstated), not re-run. GPU batch throughput against a single CPU is a cross-hardware comparison, and the 7.17x/3.79x GPU comparison is also cross-hardware (RTX 4090 vs A100). The abstract labels 58.05x/73.14x as 'over the reference', but it is really against Nguyen et al. on an Apple M1. No code is linked from the paper. The repo github.com/russdrh/FP-GOLF (on the first author's account; a CUDA Falcon port with no license, created 2026-05, 0 stars) may be related but is not confirmed as the GOLF artifact, and its Makefile flags differ (sm_80, -use_fast_math).

notes: The headline signing figure in the record (42.02 kops/s) is a 10x typo on the ePrint landing page; the PDF says 420.25 kops/s. The 58.05x/73.14x ratios are against the Apple M1 implementation, not the reference; against the reference the gain is larger (70.65x/369.13x). I kept the tier at C because of the copied, flag-less baseline and the >50x ratio, even though the paper is peer-reviewed (TIFS). I did not treat the russdrh/FP-GOLF repo as the project's code.

tier_reason: The paper was peer-reviewed (IEEE Transactions on Computers 2026) and re-ran the NIST SPHINCS+ reference C code v3.0 on one core of a Ryzen 5 5600G. However, neither the NVCC nor the CPU compiler flags/version are stated, and the gains are 1820x-3659x, so the implausible-ratio rule caps the tier at C. No code was released.

corrections.claimed_speedup: SPHINCS+-SHA256-f-simple on RTX 4090, kernel time only (memcpy excluded). Signing: 146,363 / 82,621 / 40,489 ops/s at levels 1/3/5, which is 3659.08x / 3177.73x / 3114.54x over the single-core NIST reference (40/26/13 ops/s). Verification: 1,499,590 / 933,696 / 886,362 ops/s, which is 2029.22x / 1897.76x / 1820.05x over the reference (Table VI). Against Kim et al. (open-source, re-run on the same RTX 4090): signing 1.37x/1.79x/1.58x (1.36x/1.65x/1.49x with memcpy) and verification 1.53x/1.80x/3.45x.
corrections.baseline: NIST PQC SPHINCS+ reference C code (version 3.0), SHA-256 simple fast parameter sets, run by the authors on a single core of an AMD Ryzen 5 5600G; also the open-source GPU SPHINCS+ of Kim et al. (re-run on the same GPU) plus prior GPU/FPGA works
corrections.hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (also RTX 3090 and GTX 1080); CPU baseline on an AMD Ryzen 5 5600G (single core); Linux
corrections.compiler_and_flags: NVCC on Linux (version and flags not stated); the CPU reference build's compiler and flags are not stated
corrections.workload: SPHINCS+-SHA256-128f/192f/256f-simple signing and verification throughput (ops/s) on an RTX 4090, compared with the NIST reference C code on one Ryzen 5 5600G core and with prior GPU/FPGA SPHINCS+ implementations; headline GPU numbers exclude host-device memcpy time
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed as IEEE Transactions on Computers vol. 75, no. 4, pp. 1579-1592 (2026), doi:10.1109/TC.2026.3654650; the ePrint copy is labelled Preprint and has a different title ('GRASP: Accelerating Hash-based PQC Performance on GPU Parallel Architecture'). The >1000x figure is GPU batch throughput against a single CPU core, with compiler flags unstated on both sides. The headline GPU numbers exclude memcpy. The level-3 verification figure in the text (1,408,846 ops/s) conflicts with Table VI (933,696 ops/s). No code release was found.

notes: The record's claim matches the abstract. I added the concrete per-level numbers and the peer-reviewed venue (IEEE TC 2026). Tier stays C because of the >1000x cross-hardware ratio with unstated flags. The more meaningful result is 1.37x-3.45x against Kim et al.'s open-source GPU code, re-run on the same RTX 4090.
